title: Help! I can’t decide!
bubbles: Why are you taking a raincoat?
sources: SB p.88–89, Grammar Bank 11B p.146–147; WB p.76–77

reference.title: might / might not
rows: We might have a picnic tomorrow, but it depends on the weather.
Karen might come with us tomorrow, but she’s not sure yet.
I might not take my laptop on holiday. I haven’t decided yet.
We might not see the boss today. I think she’s away.

reference.text: We use might / might not + infinitive without to to say that perhaps something will happen or perhaps it is true now: I might have a picnic = Perhaps I will have a picnic. might is the same for all persons (I / you / he / she / we / they might). might not is not usually contracted.

reference.title: may / may not
reference.text: We can also use may / may not with the same meaning: We may have a picnic tomorrow. It may not be your size.

reference.why: After might we use the verb without to.

tasks.instruction: Are you indecisive? Answer the questionnaire and ask for more information

exercises.situation: You interview the student with a questionnaire called ‘Are you indecisive?’. Ask one question at a time and ask for more information: Do you have problems deciding what to pack when you’re going away? What to buy when you go shopping? What to wear in the morning? What to order in a restaurant? Where to go on holiday? Do you often change your mind about things? What kind of things? Do you think you are indecisive? At the end, say if you think they are indecisive.
exercises.goal: Answer a questionnaire about being indecisive.
exercises.opener: Do you have problems deciding what to pack when you’re going away?
criteria: answers every question and gives examples
uses the present simple for habits (I usually…, I often change my mind…)
says if they think they are indecisive

steps.example: Yes, I always pack too many things.

steps.example: I never know what to order in a restaurant.

steps.text: Say what you often change your mind about
steps.example: I often change my mind about what to wear.

steps.text: Say if you are indecisive
steps.example: I think I’m quite indecisive.

reference.text: A diphthong is two vowel sounds together, e.g. /aɪ/ = /a/ + /ɪ/. Be careful: since /ɪ/, key /iː/, trousers /aʊ/, fear /ɪə/, where /eə/, bus /ʌ/, throw /əʊ/, and town /aʊ/ are different.

reference.title: Making nouns from verbs
reference.text: With some verbs you can make a noun by adding -ion, -sion, -ation, or -ition, e.g. decide → decision. With some other verbs, the noun is a new word, e.g. choose (verb) → choice (noun).

reference.why: pronounce → pronunciation: the noun has no o after the first n.

reference.title: Is too much choice making us unhappy?
reference.text: Nowadays there are hundreds of kinds of jeans, milk, hotels, and TV channels. Researchers have discovered that too much choice makes us stressed and dissatisfied: we worry about making the wrong decision. In a study, Professor Mark Lepper found that people who tried six kinds of jam were happier with their choice than people who tried 24. His advice: relax and choose quickly.

tasks.instruction: Look at the photos. What style of jeans do you usually buy? What colour? Do you sometimes have problems finding the right ones?

exercises.situation: You and the student are talking about jeans. Ask what style of jeans they usually buy (ripped, bootcut, straight, skinny, or boyfriend), what colour, and if they sometimes have problems finding the right ones. Ask for more details. Say that you always buy straight dark blue jeans and it takes you hours to find the right size.
exercises.goal: Talk about the jeans you usually buy.
exercises.opener: What style of jeans do you usually buy?
criteria: names a style of jeans (skinny, straight, bootcut, ripped, boyfriend)
says what colour they usually buy
says if it is easy or difficult to find the right ones and why
